items.prose: A position: buy 200 at £50.00, buy 100 at £53.00, sell 150, buy 50 at £56.00.
items.question: What is the average price at the end, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each buy by its shares; a sale changes only the quantity.

byKey.nosell: You kept all 300 shares in the last step. After selling 150, only 150 remain at £51.00.
byKey.simple: You averaged the three prices. Weight each by its shares.

explain.text: The first two buys give $(10000 + 5300)/300 = 51$. Selling 150 leaves 150 at £51.00. The last buy gives $(7650 + 2800)/200 = 52.25$.

items.prose: Extend your `Position`: `sell(qty, px)` now returns the P&L of that sale, $q \times (p - \bar p)$, and adds it to a running `realised()` total. Prices must be positive.
items.question: Write `buy` and `sell` with every check: no short sales, and no quantity or price of 0 or less. A flat position has average price 0.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and compiles in 10 to 15 s. Later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 11 hidden tests, with P&L accepted within a relative 1e-9. Four tests pass only if the program stops.

feedback.correct: Quantity, average and realised P&L stay consistent.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test under the editor.

explain.text: A sale earns $q(p - \bar p)$ against the average cost and leaves the average alone. Selling 150 at £55.00 against £51.00 makes £600; the last 150 at £49.00 lose £300, so £300 is realised.

items.prose: `Fixed<Places>` holds a value as a whole number of $10^{-\text{Places}}$ units. `Fixed<2>` is pence and `Fixed<4>` an FX rate. A different `Places` is a different type.
items.question: Write `str()` and `operator+` for two values of the same `Fixed<Places>`. In `str()`, 1234 units of `Fixed<2>` is `"12.34"`, `Fixed<0>` has no dot, and negatives start with `-`.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and compiles in 10 to 15 s. Later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 8 hidden tests with `Fixed<0>`, `Fixed<2>` and `Fixed<4>`, comparing text exactly.

feedback.correct: Exact decimals, with the places fixed at compile time.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test under the editor.

explain.text: `str()` splits the absolute units by $10^{\text{Places}}$ and pads the fraction to `Places` digits. Because `operator+` takes two `Fixed<Places>` with the same `Places`, adding pence to an FX rate does not compile.

items.question: Which change makes copying a `Prices` safe?

options.text: Replace `double*` with `std::vector<double>`, built with `data_(n)`, and delete the destructor

options.why: The default copy still copies the address, so the block is freed twice.
Then nothing is freed twice, but nothing is freed at all: every `Prices` leaks.
A const pointer still copies the same address. Two destructors free one block.

feedback.correct: Rule of zero: let a member own the memory.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Who owns the block after a copy?

explain.text: A `std::vector<double>` copies its elements, frees them once, and moves cheaply. With it the class needs no special members at all.

items.title: Designing a Position class
items.prompt:
A desk asks you to design the C++ `Position` class its risk system will use. One object tracks one instrument: the ticker, signed quantity, average entry price and realised P&L. Shorts are allowed up to a limit. It is stored in containers, copied into reports and printed in logs.

(a) State the invariants the class must keep, and say where each one is checked. (b) Write the class declaration: members, constructor, the functions that change it and those that read it. (c) Say which special members you write and why. (d) Say which operators you would overload, and which you would refuse to, with reasons. (e) Say how money is stored and how a broken rule is reported.

rubric.text: States at least three invariants and where each is checked. Examples: non-empty ticker, limit on |qty|, flat means average 0, the weighted-average rule
Data private; changes only through checked functions; readers `const`; no non-const reference to a member returned
Initialiser list used in the constructor, with the check after the members are built
Rule of zero justified from the member types; says a raw resource would need the rule of five or `= delete`
Operators: `operator<<` returning `std::ostream&`; refuses `+` on positions (or on mixed units) with a reason
Money in integer pence (or ticks) with no `==` on doubles, and a refused call leaves the object unchanged

items.title: A session range for any number type
items.prose:
A risk screen tracks the lowest and highest value seen in a session. The value may be a price, a tick count or a P&L in pence. Write one class template for all three.

- `SessionRange<T>` works for `T` of `int`, `long long` and `double`, and its two ends are private.
- `explicit SessionRange(T first)` starts a range that has seen one value.
- `SessionRange(T low, T high)` refuses a low above the high: `throw` or call `std::abort()`. Equal ends are allowed.
- `void add(T x)` records one more value.
- `T low() const`, `T high() const`, and `double width() const`, the high minus the low, exact for any two `int` ends.
- `a += b` widens `a` to cover `b` as well and returns `a` itself.
- `a + b` returns the range covering both and changes neither.
- `a == b` when both ends match; `a != b` otherwise.
- `os << r` writes `[low, high]`, such as `[99.5, 101.25]`, and returns `os`.
items.question: Write `SessionRange<T>` and its operators to the specification above.

tests.setup: SessionRange<int> a(10), b(5), c(20); (a += b) += c;
SessionRange<int> a(10), b(5, 30); SessionRange<int> c = a + b;
tests.call: std::vector<int>{a.low(), a.high(), b.low(), b.high(), c.low(), c.high()}

std::vector<int>{SessionRange<int>(1, 4) == SessionRange<int>(1, 4), SessionRange<int>(1, 4) == SessionRange<int>(1, 5), SessionRange<int>(1, 4) != SessionRange<int>(1, 5), SessionRange<int>(2, 4) != SessionRange<int>(1, 4), SessionRange<int>(1, 4) != SessionRange<int>(1, 4)}

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and compiles in 10 to 15 s. Later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 14 hidden tests with `int`, `long long` and `double` ranges. Doubles are accepted within a relative 1e-9. One builds a low above the high and passes only if the program stops. Two only compile a line: one on a `const` range, one that must be refused. No test can see whether the ends are private, so check that yourself.

feedback.correct: Correct. The ends stay in order, the operators agree, and `+=` hands back the range itself.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

explain.text: Every way to change a range goes through `add` or the checked constructor, so the low never passes the high. `+=` returns `SessionRange&`, so `(a += b) += c` widens `a` twice, and `+` takes its left side by value, so it widens a copy. `width` converts both ends to `double` first: $2{,}000{,}000{,}000 - (-2{,}000{,}000{,}000)$ is 4,000,000,000, past the `int` limit of 2,147,483,647.
